title: Ransom Note
directAnswer: Tally the letter counts of the magazine, then verify the ransom note never demands more of any letter than the magazine supplies. Count magazine letters in a hash map (or int[26]), decrement per note letter, and return false the moment a count goes negative. O(n + m) time.

remember.pattern: Frequency count + sufficiency check (counts must cover)
rules: Each magazine letter can be used **at most once** → this is a *multiset containment* check, not a set check.
Count the **magazine** (the supply), then make sure it **covers** every letter the note needs.
Fail fast: if `len(ransomNote) > len(magazine)` it's immediately **false** — the note can't fit.
Lowercase English only → an **`int[26]`** array beats a hash map on constant factors.
Decrement-and-check-negative is equivalent to compare-counts; either works, but **don't forget the negative check**.
Order and position are irrelevant — only **multiplicities** matter.
whenToUse: Check whether one multiset of characters can be built from another
'Can string A be formed using the letters of string B?' style prompts
Anagram / letter-availability problems with a fixed small alphabet
You need counts to cover (≥), not exactly match
antiSignals: Letters can be reused unlimited times → it's a set-membership check, not counts
You must preserve order or contiguity → substring / subsequence problem
Exact equality of counts required → that's Valid Anagram, use ==
Alphabet is huge/unicode and memory is tight → hash map over fixed array
remember.takeaway: Containment of one multiset in another reduces to 'for every letter, supply ≥ demand'. Count the supply once and check coverage. The same counting skeleton solves Valid Anagram (==), Find All Anagrams (sliding window of counts), and Minimum Window Substring (cover a demand set).

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you model 'each letter used once' as a multiset-containment check via frequency counts, and pick the O(n+m) counting solution over an O(n·m) repeated-search approach.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Using set membership (treating letters as reusable) instead of counts, or comparing counts for equality (==) as in an anagram when you only need supply ≥ demand.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Note the fail-fast length check, choose int[26] for the lowercase constraint, and decrement-on-the-fly returning false at the first negative — one pass after building counts.

problemStatement:
Given two strings `ransomNote` and `magazine`, return `true` if `ransomNote` can be constructed by using the letters from `magazine`, and `false` otherwise.

**Each letter in `magazine` can only be used once** in `ransomNote`.
constraints: ransomNote and magazine consist of lowercase English letters only
understanding: We must be able to spell out ransomNote by physically cutting letters out of the magazine, where each magazine character is consumed once. This means: for every letter, the magazine must contain at least as many copies as the ransom note requires. Position and order do not matter — only the per-letter counts.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can a magazine letter be reused for multiple note positions?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Each magazine letter is consumed once. That's why we need counts, not just membership — three 'a's in the note require three 'a's in the magazine.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What characters can appear?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Lowercase English letters only. That lets us use a fixed-size int[26] instead of a general hash map.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is it case-sensitive or whitespace-sensitive?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Per the constraints, only lowercase letters appear — no case-folding or whitespace handling needed here.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the magazine have to be fully used?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Leftover magazine letters are fine; we only need it to cover the note's demand.

examples.explanation: The magazine has no 'a' to supply the note's single required 'a'.
The note needs two 'a's but the magazine supplies only one. Counts must cover, and 1 < 2.
Magazine has two 'a's (and a spare 'b'); the note's demand of two 'a's is covered.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Search and Strike Out (Don't Ship)
approaches.whenToMention: Mention briefly to show progression, then immediately move to counting — the O(n·m) cost is the giveaway.
hints: Literal approach: for each letter of the note, find an unused copy in the magazine and 'cross it out'. What does 'find and remove' cost each time?
Searching the magazine for each note character and deleting it is a linear scan per character.
n note characters × O(m) search/delete each = O(n·m). Correct, but the repeated scanning is wasteful.
approaches.complexityReasoning: For each of the n note characters we scan up to m magazine characters to find and remove a copy → O(n·m) time. Mutable copy of the magazine → O(m) space.
approaches.explanation:
The most literal model is physical: hold the magazine, and for each letter of the ransom note find that letter somewhere in the magazine and cut it out so it can't be reused.

**Why it is correct.** Cutting out a letter enforces the 'use each once' rule directly — a consumed character is gone for future lookups. If at any point the needed letter isn't found, the note can't be built.

**Why it is slow.** Each 'find and remove' is a linear scan of the remaining magazine, and we do it once per note character. That's `O(n·m)`, which for `10⁵`-length strings is up to `10¹⁰` operations — far too slow. The repeated scanning re-examines the same characters again and again.

**The fix it motivates.** All that repeated searching exists only to answer 'is there still a spare copy of this letter?'. A frequency count answers that in `O(1)` after a single pass — which is exactly the optimal approach below. Naming this brute force shows the interviewer you derived the counting solution rather than memorised it.
approaches.insight: Repeatedly scanning to ask 'is there one left?' is the smell that a frequency count should replace the search. Whenever brute force re-scans for availability, precompute counts.

Forgetting to remove the matched letter, which would allow illegal reuse.
Using indexOf/remove inside the loop and not realising each is itself O(m).

approaches.name: Frequency Count — int[26] / Hash Map (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'count the magazine's supply, then check it covers the note's demand'.
hints: You only ever ask 'are there enough of letter X left?'. What structure answers that in O(1) without rescanning?
Count every letter in the magazine into an int[26] (index = ch - 'a'). Then walk the note, decrementing the matching count.
If any count drops below 0, the magazine ran out of that letter → return false. Survive the whole note → return true.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass over the magazine (O(m)) to build counts, one pass over the note (O(n)) to consume them → O(n + m) time. The count array is a fixed 26 slots → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
The problem is pure multiset containment: can the magazine's multiset of letters cover the ransom note's multiset? That reduces to one rule — for every letter, `supply ≥ demand`.

**Build the supply once.** Scan the magazine and tally each letter into a fixed `int[26]`, where `index = ch − 'a'`. Because the alphabet is a known 26 lowercase letters, the array *is* the hash map — direct indexing, no hashing, cache-friendly, and `O(1)` space (26 is a constant independent of input size).

**Consume the demand in one pass.** Walk the ransom note; for each letter decrement its slot. The instant a slot goes negative, the magazine has been asked for more copies of that letter than it had — return `false` immediately (fail fast). If the whole note is processed without any slot going negative, every demand was covered → return `true`. Decrement-then-check-negative is exactly equivalent to comparing 'have ≥ need' per letter, but it short-circuits as early as possible.

**Why this is not Valid Anagram.** Anagram demands the counts match *exactly* (`==`); Ransom Note only demands the supply *covers* the demand (`≥`). Leftover magazine letters are fine. Using `==` here would wrongly reject `note = "a", magazine = "ab"`. The distinction — equality vs coverage — is the conceptual trap.

**Fail-fast length check.** If `ransomNote.length() > magazine.length()`, the magazine can't possibly have enough total letters, so return `false` before counting. It's a cheap optimisation that also reads as careful thinking.
approaches.insight: Multiset containment = 'for every key, supply ≥ demand'. Count the supply, then either compare per-letter or decrement-and-watch-for-negative. Recognising the ≥ (not ==) is what separates this from Valid Anagram.

dryRun.intro: Build the magazine's letter counts, then decrement per note letter; fail if any count goes negative.

java.explanation: Fail fast — the magazine can't supply more letters than it has in total.
Build the supply: char minus 'a' maps a..z to indices 0..25.
Consume a copy; a negative count means the magazine ran out of this letter.
Survived the whole note without exhausting any letter → constructible.

python.explanation: Early exit when the note is longer than the entire magazine.
ord('a') is 97, so ord(ch) - 97 indexes a..z into 0..25.
Decrement the supply for each demanded letter.
Negative → demanded more than available → not constructible.

pitfalls: Comparing counts with == (anagram logic) instead of ≥ — leftover magazine letters are allowed.
Counting the ransom note instead of the magazine and getting the direction of the check backwards.
Forgetting the negative check after decrementing — the whole correctness hinges on it.

commonMistakes: Treating letters as reusable (set membership) instead of consuming counts.
Requiring exact count equality (==) like an anagram instead of supply ≥ demand.
Counting the note instead of the magazine, flipping the coverage check.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Set membership instead of counts
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A set ignores multiplicity, so it wrongly accepts note = "aa", magazine = "ab" (it sees 'a' exists). You must consume each letter once via counts.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
mag = set(magazine)
return all(ch in mag for ch in ransomNote)
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
counts = [0] * 26
for ch in magazine: counts[ord(ch) - 97] += 1
for ch in ransomNote:
    counts[ord(ch) - 97] -= 1
    if counts[ord(ch) - 97] < 0: return False
return True

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Equality check (anagram confusion)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Ransom Note needs the magazine to COVER the note (supply ≥ demand), not match exactly. Comparing for equality rejects valid inputs with spare letters.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
from collections import Counter
return Counter(ransomNote) == Counter(magazine)

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the negative check
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Decrementing without checking for a negative count never detects exhaustion, so the function always returns true.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
counts[ransomNote.charAt(i) - 'a']--;
// no check, falls through to return true

followupVariations.title: Minimum Window Substring
followupVariations.hint: Cover a demand multiset within a sliding window — coverage check at scale.

patternNote: Multiset containment via frequency counting. Count the supply (magazine), then verify supply ≥ demand for every letter — either by comparison or decrement-and-check-negative. The ≥ (coverage) distinguishes it from Valid Anagram's == (equality); both share the int[26] / Counter skeleton.
